title: Quantum Anomaly Detection in network traffic using Variational Quantum Classifiers
authors: Mir H M Ilham, Hardique Dasore, Abdulrahman Ababneh, Hafidz A Kabira, Samyam Shrestha, Jeyasri Sundar
abstract: The increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape requires more advanced network anomaly detection systems. Although, classical machine learning models are known to be effective, they reach computational bottlenecks when processing high-dimensional data. This study investigates the potential of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) for network traffic anomaly detection by evaluating four distinct Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) architectures. A synthetic network traffic dataset is generated for the evaluations. The VQC models systematically varied feature encoding methods, parameterized ansatz circuits, quantum neural network types, and classical optimizers. Experimental results show that a trade-off exists between circuit expressivity and optimization stability. Deeper circuits (VQC-4) achieved higher accuracy of upto 89.0\%, while simultaneously being sensitive to training conditions. A shallower variant (VQC-1) under performed, although it had consistent and stable optimization curves. Class-dependent biases were also observed such as in VQC-2, where the model struggled to find an effective decision boundary, and produced a large number of false negatives. The best performing model in this study (VQC-3) combined ZFeatureMap with RealAmplitudes ansatz, optimized using ADAM. Comparative analysis against classical machine learning models such as Support Vector Machine and Random Forest reveal a performance gap, where classical models are able to achieve perfect classification performance on the synthetic data. It is concluded that classical algorithms remain dominant in their ability to classify structured data with relatively simple class separations. However, due to the observed potential of certain VQC configurations to learn decision boundaries to classify data, their utility for future applications in noisier, higher-dimensional problems is highlighted.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum classifiers showed a trade-off between circuit expressivity and training stability, but classical models outperformed them on synthetic network traffic.
infographic.engineering_relevance: VQC architecture and optimizer choices materially affect anomaly detection, with no demonstrated advantage over classical baselines in this study.
method: Generate synthetic network traffic for anomaly detection.
Evaluate four VQC architectures varying feature encoding, ansatz, quantum neural network type, and optimizer.
Compare classification performance against Support Vector Machine and Random Forest models.
infographic.evidence_signal: VQC-4 reached up to 89.0% accuracy, VQC-3 was identified as best overall using ZFeatureMap, RealAmplitudes, and ADAM, and classical baselines achieved perfect classification on the synthetic data.
infographic.watch_item: Synthetic data with relatively simple class separations limits real-world conclusions; deeper VQCs were training-sensitive, and VQC-2 produced many false negatives.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Anomaly Detection in network traffic using Variational Quantum Classifiers

title: Towards Quantum Computation of Bulk FeO
authors: Daniel Staros, Federico Petrovich, Ammar Kirmani, Daniel N. Blaschke, M. Cerezo, Jian-Xin Zhu
abstract: Quantum computation offers a promising path towards efficient calculations of the electronic structure of correlated materials. The properties of iron-based materials, which are key for advancing geological and astrophysical understanding, are notoriously difficult to calculate with classical computers. However, despite the many recent advances in quantum computing on near intermediate scale quantum hardware, a full treatment of the electronic structure of high-$Z$ atoms or molecules remains challenging. Here, we investigate the ground-state properties of molecular FeO and Fe$_2$O$_2$ model Hamiltonians using classical exact diagonalization, Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD). The experimental quintet ground state of FeO is recovered classically and with quantum algorithms, while a nonet ground state is recovered for Fe$_2$O$_2$. Although raw VQE does not achieve chemical accuracy for the ground state of FeO or Fe$_2$O$_2$, SQD with two connectivity shells recovers the exact ground energy for both molecules utilizing remarkably few quantum computational resources. Overall, our results indicate that $ab \; initio$-informed low-energy models of correlated materials, combined with SQD, offer a new alternative for scaling up calculations of ground-state properties of strongly correlated solids on existing quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) recovers exact ground-state energies for low-energy FeO and Fe₂O₂ model Hamiltonians using few quantum computational resources.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining ab initio-informed low-energy models with SQD offers a potential route toward simulating strongly correlated materials on existing quantum hardware.
method: Construct low-energy model Hamiltonians for molecular FeO and Fe₂O₂.
Compare classical exact diagonalization, Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and SQD.
Use SQD with two connectivity shells to recover ground-state energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study recovers FeO’s experimental quintet ground state and predicts a nonet for Fe₂O₂; SQD matches exact model ground energies, while raw VQE falls short of chemical accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern molecular model Hamiltonians, not a full bulk FeO calculation; scalability to larger solids remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Quantum Computation of Bulk FeO

title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information
authors: Su Yeon Chang, Hailey S. Murray, Brian Barch, Greeshma Oruganti, Luis Pedro García-Pintos, Martin Larocca
abstract: Dynamical quantum simulations are commonly designed to access a particular response function or correlation function. Yet the underlying protocol prepares a family of many-body states that contains information well beyond the observable for which the simulation was originally designed. In this work, we explore the idea of using these states as laboratories for quantum information. As a case study, we consider the local-pulse protocols used to compute Green functions in finite XX and XXX spin chains, and we interpret opposite source rotations as encoding a classical bit into the many-body system. This allows us to follow how the resulting record propagates, how it is encoded across local subsystems, and how readily it can be accessed with different measurements. We also find a clear separation between representation and readout. While fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed response in the XX chain, simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of the locally available information in the XXX chain. This reversed ordering persists when we move from finite-pulse discrimination to local source-angle estimation. Going beyond the source record, the same reduced states also allow us to reinterpret results in terms of Bell state recovery and quantum communication rates, as well as providing direct access to the evolving bipartite and genuine multipartite entanglement of the system. Our results show that dynamical quantum simulations developed for response calculations can naturally be used to ask a much broader set of quantum-information questions about the many-body states they already prepare.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum simulations designed to calculate response functions also prepare many-body states that reveal how information propagates, becomes accessible, and supports entanglement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Existing response-simulation protocols could be reused to study information readout and quantum communication without designing an entirely new state-preparation protocol.
method: Study local-pulse Green-function protocols in finite XX and XXX spin chains.
Encode a classical bit through opposite source rotations and track its distribution and measurement accessibility.
Analyze reduced states for source-angle estimation, Bell-state recovery, communication rates, and entanglement.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the studied chains, fermionic covariance data exactly reconstruct the signed XX response, yet simple spin measurements recover a larger fraction of locally available information in XXX; this ordering also holds for local source-angle estimation.
infographic.watch_item: The case study uses finite XX and XXX chains, so generalization to other models and noisy hardware remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamical quantum simulations as laboratories for quantum information

title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
authors: Dayu Li, Naibin Zhou, Zhiyuan Chen, Zihua Chen, Yu Xu, Yuan Li
abstract: Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: Frequency-division multiplexing enables superconducting quantum gate operations to share control lines, with a proposed framework reducing line counts by one to two orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared microwave control could ease wiring-density and cooling-power constraints in large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers.
method: Encode gate controls in polychromatic microwave pulses.
Use band-pass filters within a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework.
Demonstrate parallel frequency-multiplexed CZ and XY(π/2) gates with 1:4 multiplexing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 1:4 demonstration reports average errors of (6.4±0.2)×10⁻³ for parallel CZ gates and (10.6±0.2)×10⁻⁴ for parallel XY(π/2) gates, with no statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated 1:4 multiplexing does not establish performance at the proposed larger scale, where frequency allocation, filtering and crosstalk require validation.
infographic.paper_title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing

title: $κ$-Parametrized Boltzmann Distribution Sampling on Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: João Marcos Cavalcanti de Albuquerque Neto, Gustavo Castro do Amaral, Guilherme Penello Temporão
abstract: Generative models use training data to produce new samples that resemble the original, with applications in classification and recommendation systems. Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are at the core of generative models but suffer from the computational intractability of training, which relies on sampling an unknown Boltzmann Distribution (BD). The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can assist RBM training, potentially providing benefits over strictly classical strategies. One particular problem is determining the quantum circuit depth for an arbitrary problem size that yields the expected sampling results. In this study, we evaluate QAOA-assisted sampling of BDs using Qiskit's Aer Simulator by analysing the inverse effective temperature of the distribution, $κ$, for tractable problem sizes. The results provide numerical evidence, based on Qiskit Aer simulations, that parameterized annealing-scheduled QAOA (PAQ-QAOA) can approximate RBM Boltzmann sampling for the tractable instances considered, while hardware performance and scaling remain open questions.

infographic.key_insight: Simulations suggest parameterized annealing-scheduled QAOA (PAQ-QAOA) can approximate restricted Boltzmann machine sampling for tractable problem instances.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QAOA-assisted sampling could support RBM training, but practical value depends on circuit-depth requirements and hardware performance.
method: Simulate QAOA-assisted Boltzmann sampling with Qiskit Aer.
Evaluate parameterized annealing-scheduled QAOA on tractable instances.
Analyze the sampled distribution’s inverse effective temperature, κ.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical evidence from Qiskit Aer simulations, not quantum hardware experiments or demonstrated scaling advantages.
infographic.watch_item: Circuit-depth requirements for larger problems and performance on quantum hardware remain unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: $κ$-Parametrized Boltzmann Distribution Sampling on Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

title: From QCCD Trapped-Ion Hardware to Quantum Compilers: Capabilities, Architectures, and Compilation
authors: Ludwig Schmid, Jurek Eisinger, Daniel Schoenberger, Christian D. Marciniak, Janine Hilder, Ulrich Poschinger
abstract: Shuttling-based trapped-ion quantum computers (QCCD) rank among the most mature hardware platforms. Existing and envisaged devices exhibit architectural differences in terms of register layout and connectivity. Platform-specific compilers are required to translate quantum circuits into resource-optimized hardware-level command chains. Hardware platforms and compiler software stacks are mostly developed independently of one another by different research communities. This work aims to bridge these communities by abstracting QCCD architectures and native operations, enabling computer scientists to address compilation problems using generic methods without requiring a deep background in the physical operating principles of the platform. The resulting design space is organized into a small set of architectural archetypes, each posing its own compilation problem. We then select and apply compilation methods to one- and two-dimensional QCCD architectures, finding that the routing overhead scales approximately cubically with the number of qubits for the one-dimensional architecture and approximately quadratically for the two-dimensional one. Extending this to compilation with a quantum error-correction layer reveals additional differences and similarities between the physical and logical levels. We conclude that co-design is a requirement rather than an option, and this work provides the vocabulary, archetypes, and compilation abstraction it needs.

infographic.key_insight: Abstracting QCCD trapped-ion hardware into architectural archetypes enables platform-aware compilation and highlights hardware–compiler co-design as essential.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Register layout and connectivity shape routing costs, so compiler requirements should inform trapped-ion hardware design.
method: Abstract QCCD architectures and native operations into generic compilation models.
Apply compilation methods to one- and two-dimensional architectures.
Extend the analysis to compilation with quantum error correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports routing overhead scaling approximately cubically with qubit count in the studied one-dimensional architecture and quadratically in the two-dimensional architecture.
infographic.watch_item: These scaling results concern the studied architectures; the abstract does not specify benchmark sizes or establish universal performance guarantees.
infographic.paper_title: From QCCD Trapped-Ion Hardware to Quantum Compilers: Capabilities, Architectures, and Compilation

title: Effective Noise Thresholds for Reliable Quantum Approximation Optimisation Algorithm under Noisy Environment
authors: Yozef Tjandra, Hendrik Santoso Sugiarto, Celine Vania Setiadi, Joanna Gracia Tan, Andriyan Bayu Suksmono
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are leading candidates for practical utilisation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors, but accumulating noise bounds the usefulness of circuit depths. For the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm (QAOA), this trade-off has mostly been addressed by searching for the best depth for a given device. In this work, we consider the inverse question: how much noise each depth can tolerate. Using GPU-accelerated noisy QAOA simulations for MaxCut on three graph families with 6 to 18 vertices, depths up to 10 and three noise channels, we fit the approximation ratios with a generalised logistic surface. We propose the effective noise threshold as the inflection boundary of the logistic surfaces, a noise boundary separating reliable and unreliable QAOA approximation regimes. In general, the threshold decreases as depth rises, indicating that deeper circuits demand for stricter noise requirement for reliable approximation. Its best and worst values over depth divide the noise axis into three regions: every depth remains effective, depth must be chosen with care, or no depth induces effective optimisation. Assessing on the ibm_marrakesh processor, although modelled gate errors understate factual noise, the threshold modeling remains beneficial in informing qualitative depth-dependence structure and identifying dominating noise channel in noisy QAOA.

infographic.key_insight: An effective noise threshold marks the boundary between reliable and unreliable QAOA approximation regimes, generally requiring lower noise as circuit depth increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Depth-dependent thresholds can guide QAOA circuit selection and hardware noise priorities rather than assuming deeper circuits improve optimisation.
method: Simulate noisy QAOA for MaxCut using GPU acceleration.
Fit approximation ratios with a generalised logistic surface.
Use the surface's inflection boundary to define thresholds and three noise-tolerance regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered three graph families with 6–18 vertices, depths up to 10 and three noise channels, with an additional assessment on ibm_marrakesh.
infographic.watch_item: Modelled gate errors understated actual hardware noise, so fitted thresholds should not be treated as guarantees of device performance.
infographic.paper_title: Effective Noise Thresholds for Reliable Quantum Approximation Optimisation Algorithm under Noisy Environment

title: Twist-controlled imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems
authors: Zhi-Yao Ning, Zi-Xiang Li, Naoki Kawashima
abstract: We construct a controllable imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems using spatially modulated local rotations without changing initial bipartite entanglement spectra and correlation magnitudes. This feature unambiguously isolates the redistribution of spectral weights as the sole driver of the anomalous relaxation. Using the compact-boson description, we reveal that these twists act as precise mode selectors: higher-harmonic twists exclusively populate high-energy standing waves, structurally bypassing slow-decaying infrared modes to accelerate convergence. We derive exact analytical crossing times for these reversals and demonstrate that intentionally reintroducing the slow-mode population systematically delays the ITME. This exact mechanism is validated beyond the fixed-point theory via calculations on interacting XXZ chains and ladders. Furthermore, a twelve-qubit simulation of variational quantum imaginary-time evolution reproduces the reversals and their controlled delay, providing a concrete route to realize this protocol in realistic quantum circuits. Ultimately, these results provide a strictly controllable and exact starting point for realizing and investigating the imaginary-time Mpemba effect, establishing a foundational paradigm to harness anomalous non-equilibrium relaxation in quantum ground-state preparations.

infographic.key_insight: Spatially patterned spin rotations accelerate imaginary-time relaxation by redistributing spectral weight away from slow modes while preserving initial bipartite entanglement spectra and correlation magnitudes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Twist-based initial-state design offers a controllable strategy for accelerating quantum ground-state preparation.
method: Apply spatially modulated local rotations to select excitation modes.
Use compact-boson theory to derive exact relaxation-crossing times.
Reintroduce slow-mode weight to systematically delay the imaginary-time Mpemba effect.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation in interacting XXZ chains and ladders, plus a 12-qubit variational imaginary-time simulation reproducing relaxation reversals and controlled delays.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and robustness to hardware noise remain unestablished by the reported 12-qubit simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Twist-controlled imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems

title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA
authors: Benjamin Rossdeutscher, Jingbo Wang
abstract: Quantum computing offers promising approaches to combinatorial optimization problems whose search spaces grow exponentially with problem size. The Closest String problem belongs to this category, which seeks a string that minimizes the maximum Hamming distance to any string in a given collection of reference strings. In this work, we present an end-to-end quantum implementation of the Closest String problem using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA), evaluating its resource requirements and solution amplification capabilities. Our automated workflow converts arbitrary problem instances into quantum circuits expressed in one- or two-qubit gates that encode candidate solutions, evaluate the objective function, and apply NV-QWOA optimisation to increase the measurement probabilities of high-quality solutions. Analytical resource estimates yield a qubit complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nm\log k)$ and a circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(pm\log^2 n + pn\log n)$, where $n$ is the string length, $m$ is the number of reference strings, $k$ is the alphabet size, and $p$ is the number of NV-QWOA iterations. We introduce a revised prescription for the phase-separation parameter, $γ$, that depends on problem size but requires no instance-specific optimization. This prescription mitigates excessive phase wrapping modulo $2π$, which can weaken the relationship between objective values and the phases guiding the optimization dynamics. Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal candidates. This work provides an explicit gate-level implementation, an improved phase-scaling method, and a foundation for hardware experiments and benchmarking against classical algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Non-Variational QWOA amplifies high-quality solutions to the Closest String problem using a gate-level workflow without instance-specific parameter optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The automated circuit construction and analytical resource estimates support hardware planning for quantum combinatorial optimization.
method: Encode candidate strings and evaluate their maximum Hamming distance to the reference strings.
Apply NV-QWOA iterations using a problem-size-dependent phase parameter to mitigate excessive phase wrapping.
Compile into one- and two-qubit gates, with O(nm log k) qubits and O(pm log² n + pn log n) circuit depth.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplified optimal and near-optimal candidates.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation-based amplification does not establish practical quantum advantage; hardware validation and classical benchmarking remain necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA

title: Decision-aware validation of zero-noise extrapolation in QAOA optimization landscapes
authors: Vicenzo Scavino Alfaro
abstract: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) is usually validated by the accuracy of mitigated observables, yet variational quantum optimization uses those observables to select parameters. We ask whether, and by how much, an accuracy gain from ZNE coincides with a worse decision. In depth-one simulations of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for MaxCut on four to six qubits, each sampled $120\times120$ landscape yields both its mean-squared error (MSE) and the ideal regret of its selected grid minimum, comparing Richardson orders one to three with unmitigated estimation at the same total shot budget per grid point. In an exploratory screen of 675 conditions, whose per-point random seeds collide, a familywise (Holm) analysis retains only four of 540 replication conditions as showing both directional MSE improvement and regret increase. A frozen confirmation with 100 fresh paired repetitions per condition reproduces all four: median MSE improvements of 7.65-73.09% accompany median normalized regret increases of only 0.0031-0.0073. We distinguish a bias route, in which residual bias reorders the mean landscape, from a variance route, in which Richardson weights amplify finite-shot noise. Exact first and second moments on a bounded control grid find no bias-route reversal: mitigated mean landscapes preserve the ideal minima, and ZNE can more than halve expected MSE, yet finite-shot selections incur higher mean regret. Decision losses that survive strict testing are few and small in this benchmark, but reproducible and not revealed by aggregate MSE. We present a paired benchmark and recommend reporting decision regret alongside estimation error when mitigation is assessed for optimization. Results concern simulated exhaustive grids, not hardware or optimizer loops.

infographic.key_insight: Zero-noise extrapolation can improve QAOA landscape accuracy while producing slightly worse parameter choices, so lower estimation error does not guarantee better optimization decisions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate mitigation with decision regret alongside estimation error, using matched total shot budgets.
method: Simulate depth-one QAOA for MaxCut on 4–6 qubits over 120×120 parameter grids.
Compare Richardson extrapolation orders 1–3 against unmitigated estimates at equal shot budgets.
Use paired confirmation runs and exact moment analysis to distinguish residual-bias effects from amplified sampling noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: All four conditions retained by Holm testing were reproduced in 100 fresh paired repetitions each, with median MSE improvements of 7.65–73.09% but median normalized regret increases of 0.0031–0.0073.
infographic.watch_item: Decision losses were rare and small; exploratory seed collisions and reliance on simulated exhaustive grids limit conclusions about hardware or optimizer loops.
infographic.paper_title: Decision-aware validation of zero-noise extrapolation in QAOA optimization landscapes

title: Analog Quantum Experiments Meet Automatic Differentiation - from Programs to Atoms
authors: Yue Shi, Pengyu Liu, Yuxiang Peng
abstract: Gradient-based optimization of analog quantum hardware poses a concrete programming problem: given an executable experiment P(θ) that returns only measurement samples, what executable experiment should the system run to obtain (d/dθ_ell)P(θ)? Conventional automatic differentiation cannot propagate through the inaccessible quantum state, while finite differences require a noise-sensitive step size and analytic gradient identities cover only parts of an experiment. We present DiffSimuQ, which shows that a broad class of open-loop analog quantum experiments is closed under automatic differentiation. A compositional transformation maps P(θ) to a derivative program D_ell[P(θ)] in the same language whose expected outcome is exactly the derivative. Only continuous evolution requires a strategy-specific rule, and we give two realizations. Our Nyquist shift rule (NSR) applies to general time-dependent evolution: we prove that the observable response to shifting the Hamiltonian along its tangent is band-limited even for non-commuting controls, enabling exact reconstruction from shifted executions. For involutory generators, a parameter-shift realization (PSR) inserts a parameter-independent operation at a sampled time. Because derivative programs remain ordinary programs, source and derivative experiments share one compiler, which reuses the source realization, lowers branches to device-ready neutral-atom controls, and selects between NSR and PSR based on estimated cost. Under device noise, the exact derivative programs differentiate the objective realized by the device, with hardware realization errors treated separately. In machine-level noisy emulation, NSR and PSR avoid the finite-difference error floor and improve closed-loop optimization; they win in complementary cost regimes, while each derivative branch at 1000 qubits add at most 0.3% to source compilation time.

infographic.key_insight: DiffSimuQ transforms a broad class of sample-returning analog quantum experiments into executable derivative experiments whose expected outcomes equal the desired gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Source and derivative experiments share a compiler that produces neutral-atom controls and selects between two gradient strategies using estimated cost.
method: Compositionally transform experiment programs into derivative programs in the same language.
Use the Nyquist shift rule for general time-dependent evolution, exploiting band-limited responses even with non-commuting controls.
Use a parameter-shift rule for involutory generators, inserting a parameter-independent operation at a sampled time.
infographic.evidence_signal: Machine-level noisy emulation reports avoidance of the finite-difference error floor, improved closed-loop optimization, and at most 0.3% additional source compilation time per derivative branch at 1,000 qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Exactness concerns expected outcomes; finite-shot uncertainty and hardware realization errors remain practical concerns, and reported evaluation uses emulation rather than physical-device experiments.
infographic.paper_title: Analog Quantum Experiments Meet Automatic Differentiation - from Programs to Atoms

title: Quantum circuit simulation with high-order optical tensor processing
authors: Yufeng Zhang, Xuhan Guo, Zixuan Ning, Zhiliang Yuan, Yikai Su, Kaizhi Wang
abstract: Classical simulation is essential for developing and testing quantum circuits, but the exponential growth of Hilbert space challenges conventional digital processors. Here, we introduce a classical optical quantum simulation architecture that treats gates and batches of input states as independent tensor dimensions rather than separate simulation instances, while mapping eligible tensor network contractions onto the same processor. Using co-designed multidimensional encoding and readout across spatial and wavelength degrees of freedom, we experimentally realize high-order tensor-matrix multiplication in a single propagation and process all computational-basis inputs for each 4-qubit gate. Using a physics-based optical propagation model, we further numerically evaluate the architecture for the Deutsch algorithm and for the tensor network of all 128 target instances of a 7-qubit Grover algorithm. These results establish a unified framework for gate-state batch and tensor network simulation, providing a route to exploit optical concurrency across quantum simulation tasks.

infographic.key_insight: A classical optical architecture accelerates quantum-circuit simulation by encoding gates and input-state batches as independent tensor dimensions and supporting eligible tensor-network contractions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spatial and wavelength multiplexing offer a route to concurrent quantum-simulation workloads without executing each gate–input pair separately.
method: Represent gates and batches of input states as independent tensor dimensions.
Co-design spatial and wavelength encoding and readout for high-order tensor–matrix multiplication in one optical propagation.
Map eligible quantum tensor-network contractions onto the same optical processor.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments processed all computational-basis inputs for each tested 4-qubit gate; physics-based numerical modeling evaluated Deutsch’s algorithm and all 128 target instances of a 7-qubit Grover algorithm.
infographic.watch_item: The algorithm-level results are numerical rather than experimental, so larger-scale hardware accuracy and performance remain to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum circuit simulation with high-order optical tensor processing

title: Generative quantum extreme learning machines
authors: Marcin Płodzień
abstract: Training the circuit of a quantum generative model is hampered by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with the number of qubits. In the present work we propose a generative protocol based on the paradigm of quantum extreme learning machines, in which the circuit is never trained. A random latent vector is encoded into a quantum state, evolved with a fixed unitary and measured, and only a linear output layer is trained. The encoding of the latent variable determines the functions available to the model, while the unitary decides which combinations of them are seen by the trained layer. With the help of Pauli propagation we show that for a Clifford unitary each feature is a single product of sines and cosines of the encoded angles, so that a Clifford circuit, even a strongly entangling one, does not create new functions. Doping the circuit with $T$ gates mixes these products and changes the nonstabilizerness of the state, but the space of functions remains the one fixed by the encoding. For brickworks of Haar-random two-qubit gates the features are no longer single products, and their variation with the latent variable decreases with the depth of the circuit. For the proposed encoding and for one- and two-dimensional distributions, generated both from expectation values and from single measurements, neither the entanglement produced by a Clifford reservoir nor the additional nonstabilizerness of Haar-random brickworks systematically improves the generator, and a reservoir with no gates at all is competitive with entangling circuits.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum generator with a fixed circuit and a trained linear output layer can remain competitive without entangling gates, while avoiding circuit-training barren plateaus.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For the tested generation tasks, simpler quantum reservoirs may reduce circuit demands without sacrificing performance.
method: Encode random latent vectors into quantum states, apply a fixed unitary, and measure features.
Train only a linear output layer using expectation values or single-measurement outputs.
Use Pauli propagation to analyze how Clifford, T-doped, and Haar-random circuits transform encoding-defined functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on one- and two-dimensional distributions found no systematic improvement from Clifford-generated entanglement or Haar-random reservoir nonstabilizerness; a gate-free reservoir was competitive.
infographic.watch_item: Findings are limited to the proposed encoding and tested distributions; deeper Haar-random circuits also reduced feature variation with the latent input.
infographic.paper_title: Generative quantum extreme learning machines

title: Equilibrium Learning of Quantum Circuits
authors: Frank Barrows, Touheed Atif, Yiğit Subaşı, Tyler Volkoff
abstract: Equilibrium learning trains a physical system using observables of its relaxed states. We extend this principle to gate-based quantum circuits by embedding a parametrized circuit in a Feynman-Kitaev (FK) Hamiltonian and imposing the compilation target either through an output clamping term or through a target-dependent cyclic condition on the clock register. The ground state energies and the overlaps of the corresponding ground states with the free history state define faithful cost functions for unitary and state compilation. We show that these costs are nonlinear functions of the compilation infidelity and therefore reshape the optimization landscape. We show that starting from the free history state, quantum phase estimation can prepare the relevant ground states and estimate the cost functions with polynomial resources. In two-qubit benchmarks, optimization with the equilibrium cost functions reaches a fixed fidelity threshold in fewer sweeps than standard compilation infidelity cost function for many instances. The results demonstrate the potential for encoding quantum learning problems as computation of equilibrium observables.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding quantum circuits in a Feynman–Kitaev Hamiltonian turns compilation into equilibrium learning, with faithful costs that nonlinearly reshape the infidelity landscape.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Equilibrium observables offer alternative training objectives for gate-based quantum compilation that may reduce optimization sweeps.
method: Embed a parametrized circuit in a Feynman–Kitaev history-state Hamiltonian.
Encode the target through output clamping or a target-dependent cyclic clock condition.
Use ground-state energies or overlaps as costs, estimated via quantum phase estimation with polynomial resources.
infographic.evidence_signal: In two-qubit benchmarks, equilibrium costs reached a fixed fidelity threshold in fewer sweeps than standard compilation infidelity for many instances.
infographic.watch_item: Two-qubit results do not establish large-scale speedups, and phase-estimation overhead may outweigh savings in optimization sweeps.
infographic.paper_title: Equilibrium Learning of Quantum Circuits

title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments
authors: Timur Javid, Brian Doolittle, Colin P. Lualdi, Brittany Conner, Michael Vayninger, Eric Chitambar
abstract: Quantum networking enables advanced communication protocols, distributed quantum computing, and enhanced sensing. These applications are often hindered by current realizations of quantum network nodes, which utilize noisy and imperfect hardware. Here, we apply variational optimization to counteract the effects of such imperfections. We parameterize network protocols for use with variational methods and then use these methods to optimize simple prepare-and-measure protocols on an optical testbed as a proof-of-principle demonstration. We demonstrate automated polarization compensation, achieving results comparable to conventional methods. We also analyze the effects of hardware imperfections and dark counts on the performance of our optimizations. We compare the performance of various gradient estimation methods and propose natural extensions, including further improvements through the use of global optimization and hybrid gradient estimation methods, as well as the application of variational optimization to nodes deployed on fiber networks.

infographic.key_insight: Variational optimization can compensate for hardware imperfections in optical polarization-qubit experiments, achieving performance comparable to conventional polarization compensation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated tuning could help quantum-network nodes maintain polarization control despite noisy, imperfect hardware.
method: Parameterize prepare-and-measure protocols for variational optimization.
Optimize protocol settings on an optical testbed.
Compare gradient estimation methods and analyze hardware imperfections and dark counts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The optical proof-of-principle demonstration reports polarization compensation comparable to conventional methods, but the abstract provides no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on deployed fiber-network nodes remains unverified, and hardware imperfections and dark counts can affect optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments

title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
authors: Chayan Patra, Prayas Ghosh, Adwait Patkhedkar, Rahul Maitra
abstract: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed quantum-centric supercomputing combines smaller quantum calculations with generative learning to reconstruct intermolecular electronic structure at lower computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Partitioning molecular systems can reduce per-subproblem qubit requirements, circuit depth, sampling budgets, and classical diagonalization demands.
method: Solve molecular fragments in parallel using physics-informed generative sample-based quantum diagonalization (PIGen-SQD).
Optimize local-to-global bit assignments to assemble a mapped tensor product state.
Use a second generative module to identify dominant global configurations and recover inter-fragment correlations.
infographic.evidence_signal: For water and formamide dimers, the abstract reports up to 95% smaller diagonalization dimensions and an order-of-magnitude improvement in energy accuracy over conventional SQD; a 120-qubit water hexamer was partitioned into six 20-qubit subsystems with excellent agreement with classical references.
infographic.watch_item: The hexamer reconstruction uses a dimeric approximation, leaving accuracy for systems with stronger higher-order inter-fragment correlations uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions

title: Meet-in-the-Middle Compilation of the $[\mathrm{CNOT}]$ Class with Fibonacci Anyons
authors: Matvei Fedin, Andrey Morozov
abstract: Compilation of two-qubit Fibonacci anyon gates is complicated by leakage ($\ell$) from the four-dimensional computational sector to the fifth state of the fusion space. We construct a GPU pipeline to find low-leakage representatives of the $[\text{CNOT}]$ class on different subsets of the braid group. We exhaustively explore the full positive five-generator alphabet up to $L=21$ with minimal leakage $\ell\sim10^{-3}$ and error $d_{[\text{CNOT}]}\sim 10^{-8}$ on it. To reach larger lengths, the search space is successively narrowed to three-generator, boundary-$σ_3$, and palindromic braids, and by considering only the Garside left normal form. These optimizations allow us to reach $L=72$. For $L=69$, a braid with $\ell\sim10^{-10}$ and $d_{[\text{CNOT}]}\sim 10^{-10}$ is found. In addition to directly enumerating optimal braids, we proved that $\ell\in\mathbb Z[\varphi]$, and any nonzero leakage obeys an exponential lower bound in the braid length, and obtained the limit laws $F_{3,\infty}(\ell)=\ell^2$ and $F_{5,\infty}(\ell)=\ell^4$ for our sets. Using asymptotics for the distribution function $F$, we showed that for sufficiently long braids, the asymptotics of exhaustive search are better than the asymptotics of random sampling for finding low-leakage braids.

infographic.key_insight: GPU-based meet-in-the-middle compilation finds Fibonacci-anyon braids in the CNOT equivalence class with leakage and class error both around 10⁻¹⁰ at length 69.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports low-leakage two-qubit gate compilation for Fibonacci-anyon quantum hardware while managing the rapid growth of braid search spaces.
method: Exhaustively search the full positive five-generator alphabet through length 21.
Reach length 72 by narrowing to three-generator, boundary-σ₃, and palindromic braids and using Garside left normal form.
Derive leakage bounds and limiting distributions to compare exhaustive search with random sampling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports leakage around 10⁻³ and CNOT-class error around 10⁻⁸ in the full search through length 21, and both around 10⁻¹⁰ for a length-69 braid in a restricted search.
infographic.watch_item: Longer-length results rely on restricted braid families, and low CNOT-class error does not alone establish a hardware-ready exact CNOT implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Meet-in-the-Middle Compilation of the $[\mathrm{CNOT}]$ Class with Fibonacci Anyons

title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory for Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics
authors: Lars Meschede, Daniel D. A. Clarke, Ortwin Hess
abstract: Cavity quantum magnonics has ushered in an unprecedented era of hybrid light-matter interfaces in which microwave photons, collective spin excitations, and superconducting or spin qubits can be coupled within a single device architecture, facilitating a versatile platform for quantum information processing. Realizing their full potential, however, requires a theory that can treat non-reciprocal magnetic media, material dissipation and open-cavity radiation losses, as well as finite-temperature fluctuations rigorously and without significant approximation. The dissipative magnonic resonances of such systems are described as quasinormal modes (QNMs), yet a consistent quantization procedure for lossy gyrotropic resonators has remained elusive. In this work, we present a finite-temperature quantum QNM theory, based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media and complex coordinate transformations, that achieves QNM quantization for a wide class of spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative and dispersive, cavity magnonic systems. We demonstrate the predictive capabilities of our theory via applications to hybrid dielectric-magnonic resonators interacting with both spin and superconducting qubits, evidencing modal interference effects, a continuous transition from coherent to dissipative coupling, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization, at both zero and finite temperatures. By addressing the intricacies of modal loss and non-reciprocity in a fully quantum theory of cavity magnonics, our approach enables the quantitative design of hybrid quantum devices that operate under realistic open-system and thermal conditions, without recourse to ad hoc quantization schemes.

infographic.key_insight: A finite-temperature quantum quasinormal-mode theory describes lossy, non-reciprocal cavity magnonic systems while accounting for material dissipation, radiation losses, and thermal fluctuations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports quantitative design of hybrid photon–magnon–qubit devices under realistic open-system and thermal conditions.
method: Combine macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media with complex coordinate transformations.
Quantize quasinormal modes in spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative, dispersive resonators.
Apply the theory to hybrid dielectric–magnonic resonators coupled to spin and superconducting qubits.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical applications showing modal interference, a coherent-to-dissipative coupling transition, spatiotemporal quantum fields, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization at zero and finite temperatures.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report experimental validation or computational scaling, leaving practical accuracy and implementation cost to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory for Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics

title: Decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification for quantum low-density parity-check codes
authors: Josu Etxezarreta Martinez, Francisco Garcia-Herrero, Ruben M. Otxoa, Reza Dastbasteh
abstract: Real-time decoding is a fundamental necessity for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. In this work, we introduce decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification (DAWG), an ensemble based approach that combines Tanner graph sparsification with ensembling belief-propagation (BP) decoders. The DAWG decoder runs BP decoders over the full detector error model Tanner graph for certain iterations to then transfer the posteriors to a sparsified graph in which additional rounds of BP are run. Each of the decoders in the ensemble uses a different transfer matrix to map the posterior information to the sparsified graph. We use the serial schedule for the minimum-sum BP decoders and, thus, employ Vibe decoding ideas by randomizing the schedules of each of them. The performance of the DAWG decoder is then numerically studied for bivariate bicycle codes and superdense color code circuits to be compared with other state-of-the-art decoding approaches. Importantly, the DAWG decoder shows a similar performance to Relay belief-propagation and Vibe decoding when combined with an order-$0$ Localized Statistics Decoding (LSD-$0$) post-processor. Crucially, the post-processor is called an order of magnitude less times than for Vibe with the same ensemble size, indicating that the introduced latency tail will be minimal. Furthermore, LSD-$0$ operates on a sparsified decoding graph of a fraction of the size of the full detector error model, which simplifies the resources required by specialized hardware to support it. Overall, the DAWG+LSD-$0$ decoder represents a viable low-cost BP-based decoding algorithm for quantum error correction codes.

infographic.key_insight: DAWG combines belief-propagation ensembles with graph sparsification to achieve competitive quantum error-correction decoding while reducing reliance on post-processing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fewer post-processing calls and a smaller post-processing graph could reduce decoding latency tails and specialized-hardware resource requirements.
method: Run serial minimum-sum belief propagation on the full detector error model Tanner graph, then continue on a sparsified graph.
Diversify ensemble members using distinct posterior-transfer matrices and randomized update schedules.
Combine DAWG with order-0 Localized Statistics Decoding (LSD-0) post-processing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies on bivariate bicycle codes and superdense color-code circuits report performance similar to Relay BP and Vibe with LSD-0, with roughly tenfold fewer post-processing calls than Vibe at the same ensemble size.
infographic.watch_item: Real-time latency and hardware savings remain to be demonstrated in implementation; fewer post-processing calls alone do not establish end-to-end speed.
infographic.paper_title: Decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification for quantum low-density parity-check codes

title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems
authors: V. M. Tkachuk, M. I. Samar
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum-classical method for reconstructing energy-level degeneracies and thermodynamic properties of spin systems. A single ancilla qubit is used to measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures. For spectra lying on a known equally spaced energy grid, the inverse discrete Fourier transform allows exact reconstruction of degeneracies in the absence of noise, without spectral leakage. The quantum circuits are optimized using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering. We demonstrate the method for frustrated Ising antiferromagnets on periodic Kagome graphs with up to 36 spins, using the ibm_kingston quantum processor. Despite substantial circuit depth and hardware noise, the reconstructed spectra retain their dominant features, and the calculated heat capacities reproduce the main temperature dependence of the exact results. Keywords: partition function, imaginary temperature, Ising model, heat capacity, ancilla qubit, quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid quantum–classical method reconstructs spin-system energy degeneracies from imaginary-temperature partition-function measurements, enabling thermodynamic calculations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Single-ancilla readout and circuit optimizations offer a hardware-tested route to estimating spin-system thermodynamics on noisy quantum processors.
method: Use one ancilla qubit to measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures.
Apply an inverse discrete Fourier transform on a known, equally spaced energy grid to reconstruct degeneracies.
Optimize circuits using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on periodic Kagome Ising antiferromagnets with up to 36 spins on ibm_kingston retained dominant spectral features and reproduced the main temperature dependence of exact heat capacities.
infographic.watch_item: Exact, leakage-free reconstruction requires noiseless measurements and a known, equally spaced energy grid; deep circuits remain vulnerable to hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems
